body:
1. **Read float tokens of 16 to 19 digits 16 bytes at a time.**
   - `layout_decimal()` combines the digits with NEON or SSE2 (`sixteen_digits()`), and `layout_float()` sends them to Eisel-Lemire directly.
   - `get<double>()` converts tokens of 16 or 17 digits without an exponent (the shape of coordinates written with full precision) with a lean Eisel-Lemire (`coordinate_float()`).
2. **Dump such tokens in batches of up to 256 ahead of the walk, one loop per step.**
   - The digits, 16 bytes at a time, and the token's last four digits.
   - `locate_token()`: Eisel-Lemire gives the double x. The position of x relative to the token is exact in a 64-bit fixed-point number, with 56 bits after the point of the token's last digit.
   - `token_digits_1/2()`, one loop per kind: the digits Zmij would write, chosen from that position. Exact ties between two candidates (like `754570942.33984373`, whose double is `...33984375`) are left to the full conversion.
   - The output is the token with its last four digits replaced. A rounding that carries further goes to the writer of Zmij's results.
   - The batch storage is allocated on the heap by the first conversion. A pair of floats like `[x, y]` in a read-only document is written without a frame.
   - Only on SIMD targets (NEON, SSE2) that are little-endian (`NLOHMANN_VIEW_VECTOR`, `NLOHMANN_VIEW_LITTLE_ENDIAN`). Other targets keep the previous code.

## Numbers

`compare.py --download --rounds 30`, Apple M1 Max, clang 21, two runs in opposite order after the rebase onto develop. json_view, and the factor of yyjson 0.13.0 over it:

| row | develop | this PR | yyjson / json_view |
|---|---|---|---|
| canada dump | 3872 µs | 1733 µs | 0.47x → 1.05x |
| canada traverse | 2455 µs | 1921 µs | 0.84x → 1.08x |
| canada patch | 4803 µs | 2814 ... 2936 µs | 0.80x → 1.39x ... 1.43x |
| canada update | 4941 µs | 3134 ... 3845 µs | 0.78x → 1.05x ... 1.30x |
| corpus citm_catalog dump | | | −8 % ... −14 % |
| corpus twitter dump | | | −4 % ... −5 % |

Linux x86-64 (Haswell VPS, GCC 13, before the rebase): canada dump 0.53x → 0.72x, traverse 0.89x → 0.95x, patch 1.01x → 1.17x, update 0.96x → 1.13x.

### Open

- Canada dump on x86-64 is still behind yyjson, but less. With GCC 13, most of the gap was branch mispredictions: GCC compiled the `?:` selections of `token_digits_1/2()`, `biased_distance()` and the batch's classification loop as branches, whose conditions are as good as random (callgrind `--branch-sim`: 220k mispredictions per dump with GCC, 97k with Clang). 9fad526888 writes them as masks (`mask_if()`, `select_if()`):
  - GCC 13: canada dump 4.74 ... 5.04 ms → 3.98 ... 4.24 ms (`dprobe`, best of 60, 3 interleaved rounds), 98k mispredictions; in `bench_all`, 0.75 ... 0.78x → 0.91x of yyjson, and now ahead of `json::dump()` and Glaze there.
  - Clang 18 unchanged (0.90 ... 0.95x of yyjson before and after); Apple M1 Max: 0.5 ... 1.8 % fewer cycles per dump.
  - The rest is the conversion: a float of more than 15 digits is converted from its text before it is written.
- Canada traverse in a build with aligned code (`-falign-loops=64 -mllvm -align-all-functions=6`) is at 0.99x.
- In `bench_view` only, twitter, citm_catalog, rpc, and status dump are 2 ... 9 % slower in both runs. The same dumps are 4 ... 14 % faster in `bench_corpus`, and a separate probe built against both trees also shows them faster (twitter 77 → 71 µs, citm_catalog 145 → 136 µs). They match with page-aligned functions, so this is code layout of the `bench_view` binary.
- The jeopardy rows of `bench_view` vary by ±40 % between runs, without a change in the parser; a separate traverse probe shows no difference (6.55 ms both).

An opt-in conversion at parse time (`JSON_VIEW_EAGER_FLOATS`) was prototyped and dropped: canada parse+traverse −4 ... −7 %, but parse+dump +11 ... +30 % and canada parse +36 ... +90 %.

## Validation

- **Differential check:** `dump()` output is byte-identical to develop for 10^9 generated tokens in one array and 3 × 10^8 in arrays of 1 to 9 elements (all exponents, subnormals, 15 to 18 digits, exact binary fractions and ties, near-short decimals), on M1 after the rebase; 2.5 × 10^8 and 10^8 on x86-64 before it.
- `get<double>()` equals `json::parse` on 5 × 10^7 values.
- New tests in `unit-json_view_dump.cpp`: the tie case, short and mixed arrays around the pair path, 20,000 random 16/17-digit pairs and objects, and an editable document.
- All json_view unit tests with ASan/UBSan, in C++11 and C++17.
- 9fad526888: `dump()` equals `json::parse(text).dump()` for 10^8 random tokens (16/17-digit, `%.17g` and short; singles and pairs): 4 × 10^7 with GCC 13 on x86-64, 6 × 10^7 with Apple clang on arm64. `unit-json_view_dump` passes with GCC 13 and with Clang under ASan/UBSan.
- Each commit's `single_include` is a fresh `make amalgamate`.
- #5890 changes `view/image.hpp` and `unit-json_view_dump.cpp` too. It merges with this PR except for `single_include/nlohmann/json_view.hpp` (regenerate after the first one lands), and the json_view tests pass on the merged tree.

## Public API

No breaking changes. No new macros; output is unchanged.

Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.

comments.body:
Independent check of this PR on the Mac, plus a profile on x86-64 that explains the remaining gap there. I'm sharing this as measurements; the numbers come from my own scripts, not from the PR description.

**Mac, develop (cc917d7123) vs this PR (e7d245db7e)**

Apple M1 Max, clang 21, `compare.py --download --rounds 30` with Boost, pinned yyjson 0.13.0 / simdjson 4.6.11. Each tree was built unaligned twice and once with `-mllvm -align-all-functions=6`. The aligned run is clean (the other engines moved by a median of 1.000 between the two trees); in the unaligned runs the other engines drifted by up to ±10 % in places, so I rely on the aligned run and on best-of-3.

| canada row | develop | this PR | json_view / yyjson (aligned run) |
|---|---|---|---|
| dump | 3.70 ms | 1.65 ms | 0.95 |
| parse+dump | 4.70 ms | 2.62 ms | 0.81 |
| traverse | 2.35 ms | 1.84 ms | 0.97 |
| patch | 4.74 ms | 2.81 ms | 0.74 |
| update | 4.89 ms | 2.99 ms | 0.79 |

No other `json_view` row of `bench_view`, `bench_corpus` or `bench_edit` differs by more than 3 % between the trees (best of three runs). Traverse and dump are within about 5 % of yyjson, so I would call them even rather than ahead.

**Output is byte-identical to develop**

A separate generator (not the one in this PR): random doubles of any exponent printed with 15 to 19 digits, 16/17-digit coordinates, exact binary fractions (ties), subnormals and extreme exponents, near-short decimals, and 18/19-digit decimals. 3 × 10^8 tokens in single arrays and 5 × 10^8 tokens in arrays of 1 to 9 elements, the same seeds on both trees:

- The FNV-1a hash of all `dump()` output is identical on develop and on this PR (`dd7cc6303791929a` and `e7bf5af4803f70b1`).
- All tokens have the same digits as `std::to_chars` (shortest), and all outputs read back to the same double. No mismatches.

**x86-64: instructions per canada dump (callgrind, Haswell VPS, GCC 13.3 -O3)**

| | instructions per dump |
|---|---|
| develop | 56.2M |
| this PR | 38.94M |
| yyjson 0.13.0 | 32.56M |

(clang 18: 55.1M / 39.87M / 31.98M.) This reproduces the 38.6M vs 32.6M in the description; the PR is about 20 % above yyjson in instructions.

Where the PR spends them (GCC, per dump):

- `convert_ahead`: 26.33M, 67.6 % of the total, about 242 instructions per float over its 108,527 floats.
- Within it, about 13.2M is bookkeeping (the scan loop 8.31M, which is about 77 instructions per float because it walks every node including the array nodes of each `[x, y]`; the locate loop 2.93M; the per-kind token loops 1.30M; `mark` 0.64M) and about 12.8M is arithmetic (`locate_token`, `sixteen_digits` at about 35 per float, `token_digits_1/2`).
- `write_token_digits`: 4.25M. `dump_text` itself: 4.56M, including about 1.9M of inline batch checks.
- Zmij's digit generation does not run at all for canada.json.
- The non-float walk costs about 2.7M here against 6.9M in yyjson, so the walk is not the problem.
- The 16-byte digit read compiles to SSE2 as intended.

Taken together, the bookkeeping is about as large as the arithmetic, and yyjson's whole float write is about 231 instructions per float against about 315 for this path. If you want to go further on x86, I would look at fewer passes over the scratch arrays, and at letting the parser mark where runs of floats start so that dump does not have to scan for them. I have not tried either.

Two caveats: `memset` (2.10M) is the zero-fill of the output string. Callgrind counts a `rep stos` per byte, so it overstates the cost, but it is real work that yyjson does not do (develop has it too). And I measured instructions only: the VPS has no PMU counters, so I cannot say anything about IPC, and I did not re-run wall-clock timings on x86.

Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.
